steps.text: The arithmetic mean is the sum divided by count. The median is the middle ordered value, averaging the two middle values for an even count; the mode is the most frequent value.
The mean is sensitive to extreme values, while the median is often more robust. A distribution need not have exactly one mode.
Do not average subgroup means without considering subgroup sizes. A combined mean requires weighting by the number of observations represented by each mean.
Choose a summary that fits the question and distribution. A central tendency alone does not describe variability, skewness or the uncertainty of a population estimate.

steps.text: A distribution describes how values or probabilities are spread. In a continuous probability density, probability corresponds to area over an interval, not the height at one point alone.
A normal distribution is symmetric and specified by mean and standard deviation. For an exact normal model, about 68%, 95% and 99.7% lie within one, two and three standard deviations of the mean.
Right-skewed distributions have a long right tail; left-skewed distributions have a long left tail. Symmetry does not by itself prove a distribution is normal.
A standard score z = (x - μ)/σ places a value relative to a specified distribution. This describes standard-deviation units, not a direct probability without a distribution model.

steps.text: Variance measures squared deviations from a center, and standard deviation is its square root. Standard deviation has the original data units; variance has squared units.
For independent identically distributed observations with finite variance, the standard error of a sample mean is σ/√n, often estimated by s/√n.

Standard deviation describes spread of observations, while standard error describes sampling variability of an estimator. A large sample can narrow mean uncertainty without shrinking individual variability.
For a fixed positive data scale factor c, standard deviation scales by c and variance by c². Adding a constant shifts location without changing either measure of spread.

steps.text: Probability ranges from zero to one. For any events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B), so overlapping outcomes are not counted twice.
For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A)P(B). Independence differs from mutual exclusivity; two positive-probability exclusive events are not independent.
Conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B) when P(B) is positive. Reversing the condition generally changes the answer.
Diagnostic interpretation depends on prevalence as well as sensitivity and specificity. A positive result is not automatically the same probability as sensitivity.

steps.text: A statistical test evaluates evidence against a specified null model using a statistic and assumptions. Prespecifying a significance level helps define the decision rule.
A p-value is the probability, under the null model and assumptions, of data at least as incompatible with the null as the observed statistic. It is not the probability that the null is true.
A Type I error rejects a true null; a Type II error fails to reject a false null. Power is one minus the Type II error probability for a stated alternative.
Statistical significance does not determine effect importance, eliminate confounding or prove a causal mechanism. Confidence intervals describe uncertainty under their model and sampling procedure.

steps.text: Read axis variables, units, scales and legend before comparing data. A truncated axis or logarithmic scale can change visual impressions without changing the underlying values.
A slope is change in vertical quantity divided by change in horizontal quantity. Its units come from that ratio, not from the visual angle of a line on a rescaled page.
Error bars can represent standard deviation, standard error or a confidence interval. Their meaning must be specified; overlap alone is not a universal significance test.
A trend in a scatterplot shows association, not a causal mechanism by itself. Tables can provide exact values when a graphic is designed chiefly to display patterns.

steps.text: Applying data requires matching a claim to the study design, measurement and population. A precise estimate can still be biased if the underlying comparison is flawed.
Relative and absolute effects answer different questions. Reducing risk from 0.02 to 0.01 is a 50% relative reduction but only a 0.01 absolute reduction.
Check denominators, missing data and uncertainty before comparing groups. A subgroup pattern can differ from an aggregate pattern when group composition changes.
A defensible conclusion states what was measured, how uncertain it is and what alternatives remain. Correlation, significance and plausibility do not individually prove causation.
